steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI paper that studies manipulative subscription and cancellation flows (the 'Roach Motel' dark pattern) on online news sites across several countries. Motivate it with the real-world problem and new regulation, then give our objectives and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: subscriptions that are hard to cancel (Amazon case, surveys, user complaints)
- Regulatory response: new laws on cancelling subscriptions
- 1.1 Objectives & Contributions

  - main contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In 2023, documents that were leaked to Business Insider suggested that Amazon designed the process of cancelling Prime subscriptions on purpose so that it would be arduous and long. The documents also showed that the company knew about consumers being enrolled in their service involuntarily and paying for it. Consumer organizations in Europe had also complained about Amazon's practices. But Amazon is not the only company that builds obstacles to keep users subscribed. A 2022 survey of 2,500 Americans showed that one-third of Americans pay for subscriptions that they do not use, and 42% feel ‘locked in’ to their current subscription plans. Another survey from 2022 showed that consumers spend 2.5x more on subscriptions than they initially think. Users who are frustrated, celebrities included (see Figure 1), go to social media and to online forums like Reddit to complain about these manipulative practices. When Nieman Journalism Lab made a call in 2021, several users said unexpected credit card charges were a reason for cancelling their newspaper subscriptions. In 2022 there were also hundreds of one-star reviews on the customer review site ConsumerAffairs that complained about subscription practices in industries like dating sites, software subscriptions, radio/TV services, weight loss and health club memberships.

Across the globe, new laws and regulations have been passed or proposed recently to protect consumers better against unfair subscription practices. One notable example of these laws is the German Fair Consumers Act, which requires a ‘termination button’ so that it is easy to cancel subscriptions. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) proposed a ‘Click to Cancel’ option for cancelling. And the UK aims by 2024 to “ensure consumers can easily exit contracts without any unnecessary steps (ideally one click)”.

## 1.1. Objectives & Contributions
- Objectives
  - motivation: complaints, regulatory changes, surge of subscriptions as business model
  - topic: problematic practices in online news subscriptions
  - prior work: dark pattern taxonomies and/or user studies (cite); little empirical work on specific patterns like Roach Motel
  - we characterize subscription + cancellation paths from five locations
  - personas: German, Dutch, English, Texan, Californian; up to ten news sites per country
  - European personas also subscribe to the same American sites -> location differences
- Contributions
  - systematic cross-country comparison of subscription/cancellation flow designs of popular news sites
  - through lens of existing and upcoming regulations
  - effort comparison: subscribing vs cancelling
  - Roach Motel still present in all jurisdictions, varying degrees
  - dataset: 100+ screen recordings + emails received during/after cancellation; resource for researchers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In 2023, documents that were leaked to Business Insider suggested that Amazon designed the process of cancelling Prime subscriptions on purpose so that it would be arduous and long. The documents also showed that the company knew about consumers being enrolled in their service involuntarily and paying for it. Consumer organizations in Europe had also complained about Amazon's practices. But Amazon is not the only company that builds obstacles to keep users subscribed. A 2022 survey of 2,500 Americans showed that one-third of Americans pay for subscriptions that they do not use, and 42% feel ‘locked in’ to their current subscription plans. Another survey from 2022 showed that consumers spend 2.5x more on subscriptions than they initially think. Users who are frustrated, celebrities included (see Figure 1), go to social media and to online forums like Reddit to complain about these manipulative practices. When Nieman Journalism Lab made a call in 2021, several users said unexpected credit card charges were a reason for cancelling their newspaper subscriptions. In 2022 there were also hundreds of one-star reviews on the customer review site ConsumerAffairs that complained about subscription practices in industries like dating sites, software subscriptions, radio/TV services, weight loss and health club memberships.

Across the globe, new laws and regulations have been passed or proposed recently to protect consumers better against unfair subscription practices. One notable example of these laws is the German Fair Consumers Act, which requires a ‘termination button’ so that it is easy to cancel subscriptions. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) proposed a ‘Click to Cancel’ option for cancelling. And the UK aims by 2024 to “ensure consumers can easily exit contracts without any unnecessary steps (ideally one click)”.

## 1.1. Objectives & Contributions

In this paper we investigate problematic practices in online news subscriptions. We are motivated by the user complaints, by the recent and upcoming changes in regulation, and by the way subscriptions have surged as a business model. Existing research usually focuses on taxonomies of dark patterns and/or user studies, but there is limited empirical research on specific dark patterns such as Roach Motel. To fill this gap in research, we characterize the paths for subscribing to and cancelling news sites from five different locations. We posed as a German, Dutch, English, Texan and Californian consumer, and subscribed to a list of up to ten news sites for the country of each persona. Our European personas also subscribed to the same American news sites, so that we could see whether subscribing and cancelling are different based on where the subscriber is.

Our main contribution is a systematic comparison across countries of how popular news websites design their subscription and cancellation flows. We look at these flows through the requirements of the relevant existing and upcoming regulations. We also compare the subscription and cancellation flows in terms of how much effort is needed to reach each of the two goals. We show that the Roach Motel is still present in all the jurisdictions we studied, though to different degrees. Finally, we contribute a dataset of over 100 screen recordings of subscriptions and cancellations, which also includes the emails we received during or after cancelling. This dataset is comprehensive and can be a valuable resource for researchers who study subscription-based services from different perspectives.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In 2023, documents leaked to Business Insider suggested that Amazon intentionally designed the process of cancelling Prime subscriptions to be arduous and prolonged. The documents also revealed that the company was aware of consumers being involuntarily enrolled in and paying for their service [1,2]. Amazon’s practices had also prompted complaints by consumer organizations in Europe [3,4]. However, this practice of building obstacles to keep users subscribed is not limited to Amazon [5,6,7,8]. In fact, a 2022 survey of 2,500 Americans showed that one-third of Americans are paying for subscriptions they do not use, with 42% feeling ‘locked in’ to their current subscription plans [9]. Another 2022 survey showed that consumers spend 2.5x more on subscriptions than they initially think [10]. Frustrated users, including celebrities (see Figure 1) [11], turn to social media and online forums such as Reddit to complain about these manipulative practices [12,13]. Responding to Nieman Journalism Lab’s call in 2021, several users listed unexpected credit card charges as a reason to cancel their newspaper subscriptions [12]. In 2022, hundreds of one-star reviews on the customer review site ConsumerAffairs complained about subscription-related practices in industries such as dating sites, software subscriptions, radio/TV services, weight loss and health club memberships [14].

New laws and regulations have recently been passed or proposed across the globe to better protect consumers against unfair subscription practices [15,16]. A notable example is the German Fair Consumers Act, which requires a ‘termination button’ to make it easy to cancel subscriptions [17]. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) proposed a ‘Click to Cancel’ option for cancelling [18]. Finally, the UK aims by 2024 to “ensure consumers can easily exit contracts without any unnecessary steps (ideally one click)” [19].

## 1.1. Objectives & Contributions

Motivated by user complaints, the recent and upcoming regulatory changes, and the surge of subscriptions as a business model, this paper investigates problematic practices in the context of online news subscriptions. Existing research typically focuses on dark pattern taxonomies and/or user studies [20,21,22,23,24], but empirical research on specific dark patterns such as Roach Motel is limited. To fill this research gap, we characterize the subscription and cancellation paths of news sites from five different locations. Specifically, we posed as a German, Dutch, English, Texan and Californian consumer and subscribed to a list of up to ten news sites for each persona’s country. In addition, our European personas subscribed to the same American news sites to observe any differences in subscribing and cancelling based on the subscriber’s location.

The main contribution of this work is a systematic cross-country comparison of the subscription and cancellation flow designs of popular news websites. We study these flows through the lens of the requirements imposed by relevant existing and upcoming regulations. We also compare subscription and cancellation flows in terms of the effort necessary to achieve each goal. We show that the Roach Motel is still present in all the jurisdictions studied, though to varying degrees. Finally, we contribute a dataset of over 100 screen recordings of subscriptions and cancellations, which also includes emails received during or after the cancellation. This comprehensive dataset is a valuable resource for researchers studying subscription-based services from various perspectives.
